claim: The RLBP1 gene encodes the 36 kDa cellular retinaldehyde-binding protein, CRALBP, a soluble retinoid carrier, in the visual cycle of the eyes.
source: The RLBP1 gene encodes the 36 kDa cellular retinaldehyde-binding protein, CRALBP, a soluble retinoid carrier, in the visual cycle of the eyes.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and introduction as established knowledge about RLBP1.

claim: Mutations in RLBP1 are associated with recessively inherited clinical phenotypes, including Bothnia dystrophy, retinitis pigmentosa, retinitis punctata albescens, fundus albipunctatus, and Newfoundland rod–cone dystrophy.
source: Mutations in RLBP1 are associated with recessively inherited clinical phenotypes, including Bothnia dystrophy, retinitis pigmentosa, retinitis punctata albescens, fundus albipunctatus, and Newfoundland rod–cone dystrophy.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature in the introduction section.

claim: Duplication of the rlbp1 gene in zebrafish resulted in cell-specific expression of the paralogs rlbp1a in the retinal pigment epithelium and rlbp1b in Müller glial cells.
source: Duplication of the rlbp1 gene in zebrafish and cell-specific expression of the paralogs rlbp1a in the retinal pigment epithelium and rlbp1b in Müller glial cells allowed us to create intrinsically cell type-specific knockout fish lines.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to Fleisch et al., 2008 and Collery et al., 2008 in the introduction.

claim: rlbp1a-mutant fish displayed reduced chromophore levels.
source: rlbp1a-mutant fish displayed reduced chromophore levels and attenuated cone photoreceptor responses to light stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC analysis data presented in Figure 2A and 2B showing reduced 11cisRAL levels.

claim: rlbp1a-mutant fish displayed attenuated cone photoreceptor responses to light stimuli.
source: rlbp1a-mutant fish displayed reduced chromophore levels and attenuated cone photoreceptor responses to light stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by ERG data presented in Figures 3 and 4 showing reduced b-wave amplitudes.

claim: rlbp1a-mutant fish accumulated 11-cis and all-trans-retinyl esters which displayed as enlarged lipid droplets in the RPE.
source: They accumulated 11-cis and all-trans-retinyl esters which displayed as enlarged lipid droplets in the RPE reminiscent of the subretinal yellow-white lesions in patients with RLBP1 mutations.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data in Figure 2 showing elevated retinyl ester levels and histological data in Figure 5 showing lipid droplets.

claim: The enlarged lipid droplets in rlbp1a-mutant fish RPE are reminiscent of the subretinal yellow-white lesions in patients with RLBP1 mutations.
source: They accumulated 11-cis and all-trans-retinyl esters which displayed as enlarged lipid droplets in the RPE reminiscent of the subretinal yellow-white lesions in patients with RLBP1 mutations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of the phenotypes observed in the zebrafish model and human patients.

claim: During aging, rlbp1a-mutant fish developed retinal thinning and cone and rod photoreceptor dystrophy.
source: During aging, these fish developed retinal thinning and cone and rod photoreceptor dystrophy.
evidence: This is supported by histological analysis in Figure 5 showing ONL thinning and disturbed outer segment morphology in adult fish.

claim: rlbp1b mutants did not display impaired vision.
source: In contrast, rlbp1b mutants did not display impaired vision.
evidence: This is supported by ERG data in Figure 3B showing no significant difference in b-wave amplitudes between rlbp1b mutants and controls.

claim: The double mutant essentially replicated the phenotype of the rlbp1a single mutant.
source: The double mutant essentially replicated the phenotype of the rlbp1a single mutant.
evidence: This is supported by retinoid analysis (Figure 2E), ERG data (Figures 3C and 4B), and histological analysis (Figure 7) showing similar phenotypes in double mutants and rlbp1a single mutants.

claim: CRALBP belongs to the CRAL-TRIO family of proteins and contains a CRAL-TRIO domain common to several lipid-binding proteins.
source: CRALBP belongs to the CRAL-TRIO family of proteins and contains a CRAL-TRIO domain common to several lipid-binding proteins (Panagabko et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Panagabko et al., 2003.

claim: In mammals, CRALBP is expressed in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and Müller glial cells (MGCs).
source: In mammals, CRALBP is expressed in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and Müller glial cells (MGCs).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge and supported by citation to Bunt-Milam and Saari, 1983.

claim: CRALBP is known to bind 11-cis-retinal (11cisRAL) in the RPE and both 11cisRAL and 11-cis-retinol (11cisROL) in the retina.
source: It is known to bind 11-cis-retinal (11cisRAL) in the RPE and both 11cisRAL and 11-cis-retinol (11cisROL) in the retina (Saari et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Saari et al., 1982.

claim: CRALBP is able to bind 9-cis-retinal but not 13-cis-retinal.
source: It is also able to bind 9-cis-retinal but not 13-cis-retinal (Saari and Bredberg, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Saari and Bredberg, 1987.

claim: CRALBP facilitates both the isomerohydrolase reaction mediated by RPE65 and the oxidation of the product, 11cisROL, to 11cisRAL.
source: CRALBP facilitates both the isomerohydrolase reaction mediated by RPE65 and the oxidation of the product, 11cisROL, to 11cisRAL (Saari et al., 2001; Saari et al., 1994; Stecher et al., 1999; Winston and Rando, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: CRALBP prevents unwanted side reactions or premature photoisomerization of the unstable chromophore 11cisRAL.
source: Also, CRALBP prevents unwanted side reactions or premature photoisomerization of the unstable chromophore 11cisRAL (McBee et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McBee et al., 2001.

claim: Mutations in RLBP1 have been associated with autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa.
source: Mutations in RLBP1 have been associated with a group of autosomal recessive retinal diseases comprising autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa (Maw et al., 1997), Bothnia dystrophy (Burstedt et al., 1999), Newfoundland rod–cone dystrophy (Eichers et al., 2002), retinitis punctata albescens (RPA) (Morimura et al., 1999), and fundus albipunctatus (Katsanis et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maw et al., 1997.

claim: Mutations in RLBP1 have been associated with Bothnia dystrophy.
source: Mutations in RLBP1 have been associated with a group of autosomal recessive retinal diseases comprising autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa (Maw et al., 1997), Bothnia dystrophy (Burstedt et al., 1999), Newfoundland rod–cone dystrophy (Eichers et al., 2002), retinitis punctata albescens (RPA) (Morimura et al., 1999), and fundus albipunctatus (Katsanis et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burstedt et al., 1999.

claim: Mutations in RLBP1 have been associated with Newfoundland rod–cone dystrophy.
source: Mutations in RLBP1 have been associated with a group of autosomal recessive retinal diseases comprising autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa (Maw et al., 1997), Bothnia dystrophy (Burstedt et al., 1999), Newfoundland rod–cone dystrophy (Eichers et al., 2002), retinitis punctata albescens (RPA) (Morimura et al., 1999), and fundus albipunctatus (Katsanis et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Eichers et al., 2002.

claim: Mutations in RLBP1 have been associated with retinitis punctata albescens (RPA).
source: Mutations in RLBP1 have been associated with a group of autosomal recessive retinal diseases comprising autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa (Maw et al., 1997), Bothnia dystrophy (Burstedt et al., 1999), Newfoundland rod–cone dystrophy (Eichers et al., 2002), retinitis punctata albescens (RPA) (Morimura et al., 1999), and fundus albipunctatus (Katsanis et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Morimura et al., 1999.

claim: Mutations in RLBP1 have been associated with fundus albipunctatus.
source: Mutations in RLBP1 have been associated with a group of autosomal recessive retinal diseases comprising autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa (Maw et al., 1997), Bothnia dystrophy (Burstedt et al., 1999), Newfoundland rod–cone dystrophy (Eichers et al., 2002), retinitis punctata albescens (RPA) (Morimura et al., 1999), and fundus albipunctatus (Katsanis et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Katsanis et al., 2001.

claim: RLBP1-associated retinal disorders all cause prolonged dark adaptation and night blindness in early childhood.
source: However, they all cause prolonged dark adaptation and night blindness in early childhood.
evidence: This is stated as a common feature of RLBP1-associated diseases based on clinical knowledge.

claim: Upon progression of RLBP1-associated disease, the involvement of the macula and RPE is possible, resulting in loss of central vision and legal blindness at the age of 20–40.
source: Upon progression, the involvement of the macula and RPE is possible, resulting in loss of central vision and legal blindness at the age of 20–40 (Burstedt and Golovleva, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burstedt and Golovleva, 2010.

claim: Patients with RLBP1-associated disease have a characteristic fundus appearance with homogeneously distributed, punctate white-yellow deposits.
source: Another interesting common feature in patients with RLBP1-associated disease is a characteristic fundus appearance with homogeneously distributed, punctate white-yellow deposits.
evidence: This is stated as a common clinical feature based on knowledge of RLBP1-associated diseases.

claim: Impaired CRALBP function can be caused by pathogenic mutations that either tighten or weaken the interaction of CRALBP with 11cisRAL.
source: It was found that impaired CRALBP function can be caused by pathogenic mutations that either tighten or weaken the interaction of CRALBP with 11cisRAL (Golovleva et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Golovleva et al., 2003.

claim: The crystal structure of wild-type and mutant CRALBP provided insights into the accompanying molecular changes within the protein.
source: The crystal structure of wild-type and mutant CRALBP provided insights into the accompanying molecular changes within the protein (He et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to He et al., 2009.

claim: A Müller glia cell-dependent intraretinal visual cycle has been proposed.
source: Besides the canonical visual cycle, a Müller glia cell-dependent intraretinal visual cycle has been proposed (Fleisch et al., 2008; Collery et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2009; Xue et al., 2015; Sato and Kefalov, 2016) as well as recycling pathways via light-dependent mechanisms both in the RPE and MGCs (Kolesnikov et al., 2021; Morshedian et al., 2019; Kaylor et al., 2017; Babino et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Recycling pathways via light-dependent mechanisms exist both in the RPE and MGCs.
source: Besides the canonical visual cycle, a Müller glia cell-dependent intraretinal visual cycle has been proposed (Fleisch et al., 2008; Collery et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2009; Xue et al., 2015; Sato and Kefalov, 2016) as well as recycling pathways via light-dependent mechanisms both in the RPE and MGCs (Kolesnikov et al., 2021; Morshedian et al., 2019; Kaylor et al., 2017; Babino et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The zebrafish eyes harbor duplicates of Cralbp and express rlbp1a in RPE cells and rlbp1b in MGCs in a nonoverlapping pattern.
source: In contrast to mammals, the zebrafish eyes harbor duplicates of Cralbp and express rlbp1a in RPE cells and rlbp1b in MGCs in a nonoverlapping pattern (Fleisch et al., 2008; Collery et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fleisch et al., 2008 and Collery et al., 2008.

claim: The cone-dominant retina of the zebrafish and the practically exclusively cone-driven retinal responses in larval stages facilitated the investigation of cone-specific defects.
source: The cone-dominant retina of the zebrafish and the practically exclusively cone-driven retinal responses in larval stages (Branchek, 1984; Bilotta et al., 2001) facilitated the investigation of cone-specific defects upon knockout of either rlbp1 paralog in larvae up to 5 days postfertilization (dpf).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Branchek, 1984 and Bilotta et al., 2001.

claim: The rlbp1a−/− line harbors a 19 bp deletion in exon four causing a frameshift and an early stop codon.
source: The rlbp1a−/− line harbors a 19 bp deletion in exon four causing a frameshift and an early stop codon.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the sequence information in Table 2.

claim: The rlbp1b−/− line displays an in-frame 18 bp deletion in exon 4.
source: The rlbp1b−/− line displays an in-frame 18 bp deletion in exon 4 (see Methods Table 2 for sequences).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the sequence information in Table 2.

claim: Both rlbp1a and rlbp1b knockouts were confirmed in retinal sections using immunohistochemistry with a CRALBP antiserum.
source: Both KOs were confirmed in retinal sections using immunohistochemistry with a CRALBP antiserum (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In wild types, CRALBP immunofluorescence is present in the RPE cells and the MGCs.
source: In wild types, CRALBP immunofluorescence is present in the RPE cells and the MGCs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A immunohistochemistry images.

claim: In rlbp1a−/−, CRALBP staining is only present in MGCs.
source: In rlbp1a−/−, the staining is only present in MGCs, while in rlbp1b−/−, staining is restricted to the RPE.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A immunohistochemistry images.

claim: In rlbp1b−/−, CRALBP staining is restricted to the RPE.
source: In rlbp1a−/−, the staining is only present in MGCs, while in rlbp1b−/−, staining is restricted to the RPE.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A immunohistochemistry images.

claim: Both single-KO lines had reduced levels of mRNA of the targeted gene, indicative of nonsense-mediated decay.
source: Both single-KO lines had reduced levels of mRNA of the targeted gene, indicative of nonsense-mediated decay (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The expression of the respective paralogs was not increased in the single-KO lines.
source: Notably, the expression of the respective paralogs was not increased.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Transcriptional adaptation through upregulation of the paralogs was not observed for Cralbps.
source: Therefore, transcriptional adaptation, often observed in zebrafish knockout models (Rossi et al., 2015), through upregulation of the paralogs, was not observed for Cralbps.
evidence: This is inferred from the qPCR data showing no upregulation of paralogs and cited reference to Rossi et al., 2015.

claim: Chromophore levels in heterozygotes were comparable to wild types.
source: Chromophore levels in heterozygotes were comparable to wild types (Figure 2A, top panel).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In rlbp1a−/− adults, 11cisRAL concentration was about threefold reduced when compared to wild-type siblings.
source: In rlbp1a−/− adults, 11cisRAL concentration was about threefold reduced when compared to wild-type siblings (Figure 2A, top panel).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In DA rlbp1a−/− larvae, 11cisRAL levels were halved relative to wild type.
source: In DA rlbp1a−/− larvae, 11cisRAL levels were halved relative to wild type (Figure 2B, top panel).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Wild-type larvae maintained high levels of 11cisRAL even upon prolonged exposure to BL.
source: In line with previous reports (Babino et al., 2015), wild-type larvae maintained high levels of 11cisRAL even upon prolonged exposure to BL (Figure 2B, top panel).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2B and citation to Babino et al., 2015.

claim: After one hour of redark adaptation, wild-type larvae regenerated the chromophore to levels of dark-adapted animals.
source: After one hour of redark adaptation, wild-type larvae regenerated the chromophore to levels of dark-adapted animals.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In rlbp1a−/− larvae, ambient illumination caused a steep decline of 11cisRAL when compared to controls.
source: In rlbp1a−/− larvae, ambient illumination caused a steep decline of 11cisRAL when compared to controls.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: After 1 hr of BL bleach, 11cisRAL levels were further reduced in rlbp1a−/− larvae.
source: After 1 hr of BL bleach, 11cisRAL levels were further reduced.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Upon redark adaption, rlbp1a−/− larvae regenerated 11cisRAL to only 57% of the level observed in dark-adapted larvae.
source: Upon redark adaption, rlbp1a−/− larvae regenerated 11cisRAL to only 57% of the level observed in dark-adapted larvae.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Eyes of adult rlbp1a−/− fish displayed significantly higher 11cisRE concentrations than their wild type and heterozygous siblings.
source: Eyes of adult rlbp1a−/− fish displayed significantly higher 11cisRE concentrations than their wild type and heterozygous siblings (Figure 2A, middle panel).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Illumination with BL led to a decrease in 11cisRE in both wild type and rlbp1a−/− larvae.
source: Illumination with BL led to a decrease in 11cisRE in both wild type and rlbp1a−/− larvae (Figure 2B, middle panel).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The esters were hydrolyzed upon light exposure but were not utilized for 11cisRAL production in rlbp1a−/− larvae.
source: Based on this observation and the reduced chromophore concentration in rlbp1a−/− larvae we assume that the esters were hydrolyzed upon light exposure but were not utilized for 11cisRAL production.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 11cisRE decreased but 11cisRAL did not increase proportionally in rlbp1a−/− larvae upon light exposure.

claim: rlbp1a−/− adult fish displayed an increased concentration of atRE.
source: Instead, we observed an increased concentration of atRE in rlbp1a−/− adult fish (Figure 2A, bottom panel) and a slight increase upon light exposure in rlbp1a−/− larvae (Figure 2B, bottom panel).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: rlbp1a−/− larvae displayed a slight increase in atRE upon light exposure.
source: Instead, we observed an increased concentration of atRE in rlbp1a−/− adult fish (Figure 2A, bottom panel) and a slight increase upon light exposure in rlbp1a−/− larvae (Figure 2B, bottom panel).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: rlbp1a−/− adult and larval fish display a significant reduction of 11cisRAL concentration under all light conditions.
source: Together, our biochemical analyses showed that rlbp1a−/− adult and larval fish display a significant reduction of 11cisRAL concentration under all light conditions and an accumulation of 11-cis and atRE.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: rlbp1a−/− adult and larval fish display an accumulation of 11-cis and atRE.
source: Together, our biochemical analyses showed that rlbp1a−/− adult and larval fish display a significant reduction of 11cisRAL concentration under all light conditions and an accumulation of 11-cis and atRE.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Comparable amounts of 11cisRAL were detected in rlbp1b−/−, rlbp1b+/−, and wild-type siblings.
source: We detected comparable amounts of 11cisRAL in rlbp1b−/−, rlbp1b+/−, and wild-type siblings (Figure 2C, top panel).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The eyes of the rlbp1b−/− and rlbp1b±fish displayed lower 11cisRE and atRE levels than the wild-type control siblings.
source: The eyes of the rlbp1b−/− and rlbp1b±fish displayed lower 11cisRE and atRE levels than the wild-type control siblings (Figure 2C, middle and bottom panel).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Genetic disruption of rlbp1b did not alter 11cisRAL concentrations in DA, bleached, and bleached and redark-adapted rlbp1b−/− larvae when compared to controls.
source: We observed that genetic disruption of rlbp1b did not alter 11cisRAL concentrations in DA, bleached, and bleached and redark-adapted rlbp1b−/− larvae when compared to controls (Figure 2D, top panel).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Retinyl ester levels at 5 dpf were not significantly altered in rlbp1b−/− larvae.
source: Also, retinyl ester levels at this stage were not significantly altered (Figure 2D, middle and bottom panel).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Adult double mutant fish displayed a reduction in 11cisRAL levels.
source: In adult double mutant fish, we found a reduction in 11cisRAL levels (Figure 2E, top panel).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Adult double mutant fish displayed high levels of RE.
source: Additionally, these fish displayed high levels of RE (Figure 2E, middle and bottom panel).
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: rlbp1b deficiency did not affect ocular retinoid concentration in such a dramatic fashion as observed in rlbp1a-deficient eyes.
source: In conclusion, rlbp1b deficiency did not affect ocular retinoid concentration in such a dramatic fashion as observed in rlbp1a-deficient eyes.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the HPLC data for rlbp1b mutants (Figure 2C and D) with rlbp1a mutants (Figure 2A and B).

claim: The double mutant displayed decreased 11cisRAL and elevated RE concentrations when compared to wild-type controls.
source: Additionally, the double mutant displayed decreased 11cisRAL and elevated RE concentrations when compared to wild-type controls.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The pattern of alterations in ocular retinoid content in the double mutant was comparable to that found in rlbp1a−/− fish.
source: This pattern of alterations in ocular retinoid content was comparable to that found in rlbp1a−/− fish.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the HPLC data for double mutants (Figure 2E) with rlbp1a mutants (Figure 2A).

claim: At 5 dpf, ERG responses are exclusively cone driven in zebrafish.
source: At this developmental stage, ERG responses are exclusively cone driven in zebrafish (Branchek, 1984; Bilotta et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Branchek, 1984 and Bilotta et al., 2001.

claim: There was a significant effect of genotype on b-wave amplitude in the rlbp1a-mutant line.
source: We found a significant effect of genotype on b-wave amplitude in the rlbp1a-mutant line.
evidence: This is supported by ERG data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In rlbp1a−/− larvae, b-wave amplitudes were significantly reduced when compared to heterozygous and wild-type siblings.
source: In rlbp1a−/− larvae, amplitudes were significantly reduced when compared to heterozygous and wild-type siblings (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Knockout of rlbp1b did not affect ERG responses under the applied conditions.
source: Knockout of rlbp1b did not affect ERG responses under the applied conditions (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The prolonged illumination reduced the sensitivity in mutant and wild-type larvae when compared to the DA state.
source: The prolonged illumination reduced the sensitivity in mutant and wild-type larvae when compared to the DA state.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing ERG responses under different light conditions shown in Figure 4.

claim: The responses of rlbp1a−/− were diminished under all light conditions when compared to wild types.
source: The responses of rlbp1a−/− were diminished under all light conditions when compared to wild types.
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The sensitivity was shifted approximately one log unit in rlbp1a−/− and the maximum amplitude remained below wild-type levels in all illumination conditions examined.
source: The sensitivity was shifted approximately one log unit and the maximum amplitude remained below wild-type levels in all illumination conditions examined.
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The responses of cone photoreceptors were not completely absent in the rlbp1a mutant, even after exposure to bright bleaching light.
source: Notably, the responses of cone photoreceptors were not completely absent in the mutant, even after exposure to bright bleaching light.
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Substantial recovery of retinal function was observed in rlbp1a−/− following redark adaptation, albeit with reduced sensitivity.
source: Also, we observed substantial recovery of retinal function following redark adaptation, albeit with reduced sensitivity.
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: DA double-KO responses showed a one log unit shift in sensitivity and reduced maximum amplitudes.
source: Again, we found a one log unit shift in sensitivity and reduced maximum amplitudes in DA double-KO responses (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Under photopic conditions, the phenotype of double-KO was similar to the one seen in rlbp1a−/−.
source: Also under photopic conditions (Figure 4B), the phenotype was similar to the one seen in rlbp1a−/−.
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Immediately after a strong bleach and following redark adaptation, the sensitivity shifted more than one log unit in double-KO compared to the respective wild-type controls.
source: However, immediately after a strong bleach, but also following redark adaptation, the sensitivity shifted more than one log unit in double-KO compared to the respective wild-type controls.
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Responses were severely attenuated but still recordable at 100 % light intensity in the bleach condition in double-KO.
source: Interestingly, responses were severely attenuated but still recordable at 100 % light intensity in the bleach condition.
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Cone function depends on RPE-expressed Cralbpa.
source: Together, our analyses demonstrated that cone function depends on RPE-expressed Cralbpa.
evidence: This is inferred from the ERG data showing reduced cone responses in rlbp1a mutants but not in rlbp1b mutants.

claim: No pronounced changes of cone responses were observed in DA Cralbpb-deficient larval eyes.
source: We observed no pronounced changes of cone responses in DA Cralbpb-deficient larval eyes and only a minor additive effect in the double mutant under the applied conditions.
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Only a minor additive effect was observed in the double mutant under the applied conditions.
source: We observed no pronounced changes of cone responses in DA Cralbpb-deficient larval eyes and only a minor additive effect in the double mutant under the applied conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing ERG data of double mutants (Figures 3C and 4B) with rlbp1a single mutants (Figures 3A and 4A).

claim: Histological examination of rlbp1a−/− larvae at 5 dpf revealed an overall normal stratification of the different retinal layers.
source: Histological examination of rlbp1a−/− larvae at 5 dpf revealed an overall normal stratification of the different retinal layers (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: In the ventral retinal periphery of rlbp1a−/− larvae at 5 dpf, fewer rod outer segments were found, indicating either slower development or an early loss of rod outer segments.
source: In the ventral retinal periphery, we found fewer rod outer segments (Figure 5, black arrows), indicating either slower development or an early loss of rod outer segments (OSs).
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 5 and is an inference based on the observation.

claim: The decrease in rhodopsin mRNA levels at 5 dpf supports the observation of fewer rod outer segments in rlbp1a−/− larvae.
source: This observation is further supported by the decrease in rhodopsin mRNA levels at this age Figure 6A.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The thickness of the outer nuclear layer (ONL) was unchanged in rlbp1a−/− larvae at 5 dpf.
source: The thickness of the outer nuclear layer (ONL), containing the photoreceptor nuclei, was unchanged (Figure 5G1).
evidence: This is supported by ONL thickness measurements shown in Figure 5G1.

claim: Already at 5 dpf, round subretinal lesions became detectable in rlbp1a−/− that appeared colorless upon staining with Richardson's solution.
source: However, already at this developmental stage, round subretinal lesions became detectable that appeared colorless upon staining with Richardson's solution (Figure 5B2 and H1).
evidence: This is supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 5B2 and H1.

claim: The subretinal lesions phenotype became more apparent at 34 dpf and in 6-month-old rlbp1a−/− fish.
source: This phenotype became more apparent at 34 dpf (Figure 5C, D and H2) and in 6-month-old fish (Figure 5E, F and H3).
evidence: This is supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 5.

claim: The subretinal lesions appeared to increase not only in number but also in size with age in rlbp1a−/−.
source: The lesions appeared to increase not only in number but also in size.
evidence: This is supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 5.

claim: Subretinal lesions were occasionally detected in wild-type siblings, but these tended to be smaller and sparser.
source: Occasionally, we detected these structures in wild-type siblings (Figure 5C2). However, these tended to be smaller and sparser.
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 5C2.

claim: Already at 34 dpf, the OSs of both rods and cones were severely shortened, dysmorphic, or sometimes completely absent in rlbp1a−/−.
source: Importantly, we also found that already at 34 dpf, the OSs of both rods and cones were severely shortened, dysmorphic, or sometimes completely absent (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The double-KO largely recapitulated the findings in rlbp1a−/− fish.
source: The double-KO (Figure 7) largely recapitulated the findings in rlbp1a−/− fish.
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 7.

claim: In adults, it appeared that rod outer segments were slightly better preserved in double-KO than in the rlbp1a−/− single mutant.
source: In adults, it appeared that rod outer segments were slightly better preserved in double-KO than in the rlbp1a−/− single mutant (compare Figures 5F, 7F).
evidence: This is inferred from comparing histological images in Figures 5F and 7F.

claim: Analysis of rhodopsin mRNA expression revealed lower expression at 5 dpf and in adults in both rlbp1a−/− single and double-KO.
source: Analysis of rhodopsin mRNA expression revealed lower expression at 5 dpf and in adults in both rlbp1a−/− single and double-KO.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The reduction of rhodopsin mRNA expression in rlbp1a−/− adults was ~ fourfold whereas in the double-KO it was roughly twofold.
source: However, the reduction of rhodopsin mRNA expression in rlbp1a−/− adults was ~ fourfold whereas in the double-KO it was roughly twofold Figure 8B,D.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6B and D.

claim: Even though the number of white lesions was comparable to the single-KO, they appeared slightly smaller in the double-KO.
source: Also, even though the number of white lesions was comparable to the single-KO, they appeared slightly smaller in the double-KO.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing histological images in Figures 5 and 7.

claim: Subretinal lesions were rare in rlbp1b+/+ and rlbp1b−/− fish.
source: Notably, these subretinal lesions were rare (Figure 8) and ONL thickness was maintained (Figure 8E) in rlbp1b+/+ and rlbp1b−/− fish.
evidence: This is supported by histological images and quantification shown in Figure 8.

claim: ONL thickness was maintained in rlbp1b+/+ and rlbp1b−/− fish.
source: Notably, these subretinal lesions were rare (Figure 8) and ONL thickness was maintained (Figure 8E) in rlbp1b+/+ and rlbp1b−/− fish.
evidence: This is supported by ONL thickness measurements shown in Figure 8E.

claim: RPE cells form lipid droplet-like structures called retinosomes.
source: RPE cells form lipid droplet-like structures called retinosomes (Imanishi et al., 2004a; Imanishi et al., 2004b; Palczewska et al., 2010; Orban et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Retinosomes serve as storage sites for retinyl esters.
source: They serve as storage sites for retinyl esters and can be visualized with lipophilic dyes, similar to other lipid droplets.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge based on cited literature.

claim: Retinosomes can be visualized with lipophilic dyes, similar to other lipid droplets.
source: They serve as storage sites for retinyl esters and can be visualized with lipophilic dyes, similar to other lipid droplets.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: An increased amount of very bright spherical structures positive for BODIPY staining were found in the subretinal space in rlbp1a−/− and double-KO retinas.
source: Indeed, we found an increased amount of very bright spherical structures positive for BODIPY staining in the subretinal space in rlbp1a−/− and double-KO retinas (Figures 5 and 7).
evidence: This is supported by BODIPY staining images shown in Figures 5I and 7I.

claim: BODIPY-positive droplets were rarely present in wild types and rlbp1b−/− fish.
source: These droplets were rarely present in wild types (Figures 5, 7, 8G) and rlbp1b−/− fish (Figure 8G).
evidence: This is supported by BODIPY staining images shown in Figures 5, 7, and 8G.

claim: Cones in the zebrafish retina rely on RPE-expressed Cralbpa for chromophore regeneration and retinal function.
source: Our results showed that cones in the zebrafish retina rely on RPE-expressed Cralbpa for chromophore regeneration and retinal function.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results of retinoid analysis and ERG measurements showing reduced chromophore levels and impaired cone function in rlbp1a mutants.

claim: The knockout of rlbp1a impaired cone-driven ERG responses.
source: We found that the knockout of rlbp1a impaired cone-driven ERG responses and led to disturbed OS morphology of both rods and cones and age-dependent thinning of the photoreceptor nuclear layer.
evidence: This is supported by ERG data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The knockout of rlbp1a led to disturbed OS morphology of both rods and cones.
source: We found that the knockout of rlbp1a impaired cone-driven ERG responses and led to disturbed OS morphology of both rods and cones and age-dependent thinning of the photoreceptor nuclear layer.
evidence: This is supported by histological images shown in Figure 5.

claim: The knockout of rlbp1a led to age-dependent thinning of the photoreceptor nuclear layer.
source: We found that the knockout of rlbp1a impaired cone-driven ERG responses and led to disturbed OS morphology of both rods and cones and age-dependent thinning of the photoreceptor nuclear layer.
evidence: This is supported by ONL thickness measurements shown in Figure 5G.

claim: HPLC analysis of rlbp1a−/− revealed an accumulation of retinyl esters and a reduction in 11cisRAL that was associated with visual impairment.
source: HPLC analysis of rlbp1a−/− revealed an accumulation of retinyl esters and a reduction in 11cisRAL that was associated with this visual impairment.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2.

claim: This study presents the first animal model that recapitulates both the age-dependent retinal thinning and the appearance of subretinal lesions that are commonly found in patients suffering from RLBP1 mutations.
source: To our knowledge, we present the first animal model that recapitulates both the age-dependent retinal thinning and the appearance of subretinal lesions that are commonly found in patients suffering from RLBP1 mutations.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the model based on comparison with prior literature and the observed phenotypes.

claim: In early stages, the lack of 11cisRAL is most likely the primary cause for the reduction in cone-mediated retinal function in the rlbpa1−/− fish.
source: Our data indicate that in early stages, the lack of 11cisRAL (Figure 2A, B and E, top panel) is most likely the primary cause for the reduction in cone-mediated retinal function in the rlbpa1−/− fish.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between reduced 11cisRAL levels and impaired ERG responses in early stages.

claim: At later stages, the disturbed OS morphology and the loss of photoreceptors are likely to contribute to a deterioration of vision in rlbp1a−/− fish.
source: However, at later stages, the disturbed OS morphology and the loss of photoreceptors are likely to contribute to a deterioration of vision in these fish.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of progressive photoreceptor degeneration in older fish.

claim: The integrity of both rods and cones is affected in rlbp1a−/− and double-KO fish.
source: In addition, it seemed that the integrity of both rods and cones is affected in rlbp1a−/− and double-KO fish.
evidence: This is supported by histological observations showing disturbed outer segments of both rods and cones.

claim: The elevated retinyl ester levels in rlbp1a−/− and double-KO zebrafish display as enlarged retinosomes found upon histological examination.
source: The elevated retinyl ester levels in rlbp1a−/− and double-KO zebrafish (Figure 2A, B and E, middle and lower panel) display as enlarged retinosomes found upon histological examination.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between elevated retinyl ester levels measured by HPLC and the presence of lipid droplets observed histologically.

claim: ONL thinning appeared, concomitant with the increased number of enlarged retinosomes, only with age.
source: ONL thinning appeared, concomitant with the increased number of enlarged retinosomes, only with age.
evidence: This is supported by the temporal correlation observed in histological data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Chromophore regeneration was not completely blocked but only attenuated in Cralbpa deficiency.
source: It is interesting to note, that chromophore regeneration was not completely blocked but only attenuated in Cralbpa deficiency.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some 11cisRAL is still present and ERG responses are still recordable in rlbp1a mutants.

claim: Chromophore regeneration was not completely blocked but only attenuated in the double-KO.
source: This was true not only for rlbp1a−/−, but also for the double-KO.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that some 11cisRAL is still present and ERG responses are still recordable in double-KO.

claim: The findings are consistent with the prolonged dark adaptation in patients with Bothnia dystrophy.
source: These findings are consistent with the prolonged dark adaptation in patients with Bothnia dystrophy (Burstedt et al., 2003), and in mouse models (Saari et al., 2001; Lima de Carvalho et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of the phenotypes and supported by citations.

claim: CRALBP facilitates the hydrolysis of 11cisRE.
source: Previously, Stecher et al., 1999 proposed that CRALBP facilitates the hydrolysis of 11cisRE.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Stecher et al., 1999.

claim: The 11cisRE pool in the zebrafish RPE is mobilized in a light-dependent manner to meet the high demand for chromophore under bright daylight conditions.
source: More recently, it was reported that the 11cisRE pool in the zebrafish RPE is mobilized in a light-dependent manner to meet the high demand for chromophore under bright daylight conditions (Babino et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Babino et al., 2015.

claim: The mobilization of the 11cisRE pool is Cralbpa dependent and plays a critical role for cone visual pigment regeneration.
source: We now demonstrated that the mobilization of the 11cisRE pool is Cralbpa dependent and plays a critical role for cone visual pigment regeneration.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 11cisRE accumulates and 11cisRAL is reduced in rlbp1a mutants.

claim: 11cisRE concentrations declined in the absence of Cralbpa upon light exposure.
source: Interestingly, we found that 11cisRE concentrations also declined in the absence of Cralbpa upon light exposure.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 11cisRE hydrolysis can occur Cralbpa independently.
source: This result raises the possibility that 11cisRE hydrolysis can occur Cralbpa independently.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that 11cisRE decreases even in the absence of Cralbpa.

claim: Cralbpa may be mainly required to assist the oxidation of 11cisROL to 11cisRAL.
source: Thus, Cralbpa may be mainly required to assist the oxidation of 11cisROL to 11cisRAL, as earlier proposed by Saari et al., 1994.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the data and supported by citation to Saari et al., 1994.

claim: Cralbpa may act as a chaperone for chromophores in the RPE and prevent the light-dependent isomerization of the released 11-cis-ROL diastereomer to the trans-diastereomer of retinol in the RPE.
source: Additionally, Cralbpa may act as a chaperone for chromophores in the RPE and prevent the light-dependent isomerization of the released 11-cis-ROL diastereomer to the trans-diastereomer of retinol in the RPE.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known function of CRALBP and the observed accumulation of atRE.

claim: The trans-diastereomer of retinol would be reesterified by LRAT, an enzyme that has a high capacity for RE production.
source: The latter would be reesterified by LRAT (lecithin retinol acyltransferase), an enzyme that has a high capacity for RE production.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about LRAT function.

claim: The increase in atRE concentration in illuminated rlbp1a−/− larvae can be explained by the light-dependent isomerization of 11-cis-ROL to trans-retinol followed by reesterification by LRAT.
source: This reaction sequence would explain the increase in atRE concentration in illuminated rlbp1a−/− larvae.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the proposed mechanism.

claim: RPE-expressed Cralbpa is found at a convergence point for potentially all chromophore producing pathways of the RPE.
source: As an acceptor of 11-cis-retinoids RPE-expressed Cralbpa is found at a convergence point for potentially all chromophore producing pathways of the RPE.
evidence: This is inferred from the known functions of CRALBP in multiple pathways.

claim: CRALBP was shown to support photic chromophore regeneration by RGR in bovine RPE.
source: Besides its well-known function in the classical visual cycle downstream of RPE65 and its role in the light-dependent 11cisRE mobilization described in this study CRALBP was also shown to support photic chromophore regeneration by RGR in bovine RPE (Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: Knockout of MGC-expressed rlbp1b in zebrafish did not affect 11cisRAL content.
source: On the other hand, knockout of MGC-expressed rlbp1b in zebrafish did not affect 11cisRAL content, nor morphology and only marginally affected retinal function in the double-KO in BL conditions.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data (Figure 2D) and ERG data (Figure 3B).

claim: Knockout of MGC-expressed rlbp1b in zebrafish did not affect morphology.
source: On the other hand, knockout of MGC-expressed rlbp1b in zebrafish did not affect 11cisRAL content, nor morphology and only marginally affected retinal function in the double-KO in BL conditions.
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Knockout of MGC-expressed rlbp1b in zebrafish only marginally affected retinal function in the double-KO in BL conditions.
source: On the other hand, knockout of MGC-expressed rlbp1b in zebrafish did not affect 11cisRAL content, nor morphology and only marginally affected retinal function in the double-KO in BL conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing ERG data of double-KO (Figure 4B) with rlbp1a single mutant (Figure 4A).

claim: MGC-expressed Cralbp does not carry out the same function in chromophore regeneration as its counterpart in the RPE.
source: This observation excludes that the MGC-expressed Cralbp carries out the same function in chromophore regeneration as its counterpart in the RPE.
evidence: This is inferred from the different phenotypes observed in rlbp1a and rlbp1b mutants.

claim: 11cisRE was mostly present in retinosomes of the RPE.
source: Accordingly, it was previously shown that 11cisRE was mostly present in retinosomes of the RPE (Babino et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Babino et al., 2015.

claim: Cralbpb may play different roles in the visual cycle.
source: However, we do not close out that Cralbpb may play different roles in the visual cycle.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential alternative functions of Cralbpb.

claim: CRALBP in MGCs could serve as a chromophore storage site by binding 11-cis-retinoids.
source: For instance, Kiser et al., 2018 suggested that CRALBP in MGCs could serve as a chromophore storage site by binding 11-cis-retinoids.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kiser et al., 2018.

claim: RGR in MGCs was implicated in light-dependent chromophore regeneration.
source: Also, RGR in MGCs was implicated in light-dependent chromophore regeneration (Morshedian et al., 2019) and Cralbpb may drive this reaction during BL conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Morshedian et al., 2019.

claim: Cralbpb may drive RGR-mediated chromophore regeneration during BL conditions.
source: Also, RGR in MGCs was implicated in light-dependent chromophore regeneration (Morshedian et al., 2019) and Cralbpb may drive this reaction during BL conditions.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential role of Cralbpb.

claim: Measurements of 11cisRAL in the rlbp1b-KO could be masked by RGR-bound retinoids.
source: In this line of thought our measurements of 11cisRAL in the rlbp1b-KO could be masked by RGR-bound retinoids and provide an explanation for the more severe phenotype in double-KO, despite the apparently normal amounts of 11cisRAL in rlbp1b-KO.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the discrepancy between retinoid levels and phenotype.

claim: Early work in mice failed to reproduce the progressive loss of photoreceptors as well as the characteristic fundus findings seen in patients.
source: Early work in mice failed to reproduce the progressive loss of photoreceptors as well as the characteristic fundus findings seen in patients (Saari et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Saari et al., 2001.

claim: A more recent study reported ONL thinning in Rlbp1−/− mice between 8 and 12 months of age.
source: A more recent study (Lima de Carvalho et al., 2020) reported ONL thinning in Rlbp1−/− mice between 8 and 12 months of age.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lima de Carvalho et al., 2020.

claim: Such changes may have gone unnoticed in earlier studies on Rlbp1−/− mice due to the younger age of animals at examination (5.5 months).
source: Such changes may have gone unnoticed in earlier studies on Rlbp1−/− mice due to the younger age of animals at examination (5.5 months).
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the discrepancy between earlier and more recent mouse studies.

claim: The onset of degenerative processes can vary between individuals in patients.
source: Also in patients, the onset of degenerative processes can vary between individuals.
evidence: This is stated as clinical knowledge.

claim: The zebrafish model recapitulates the early impairment of rods and subsequent cone dysfunction that culminates in photoreceptor degeneration at a relatively early age.
source: Our zebrafish model recapitulates the early impairment of rods and subsequent cone dysfunction that culminates in photoreceptor degeneration at a relatively early age.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed phenotypes in the zebrafish model.

claim: The zebrafish model resembles more closely an early-onset form of CRALBP-associated diseases, such as RPA or Bothnia dystrophy.
source: Therefore, it resembles more closely an early-onset form of CRALBP-associated diseases, such as RPA or Bothnia dystrophy.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of the zebrafish phenotype with human disease characteristics.

claim: The white-yellow fundus lesions in patients with CRALBP-associated disease are usually found upon imaging the central retina, including the macular region and optic disc.
source: The white-yellow fundus lesions in patients with CRALBP-associated disease are usually found upon imaging the central retina, including the macular region and optic disc (Burstedt and Golovleva, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burstedt and Golovleva, 2010.

claim: The lesions appear to be restricted in size towards the center of the retina.
source: The lesions appear to be restricted in size towards the center.
evidence: This is stated as a clinical observation.

claim: The white dots are often reported to be absent in the macula or at least the fovea.
source: Interestingly, the white dots are often reported to be absent in the macula (Demirci et al., 2004; Naz et al., 2011) or at least the fovea (Dessalces et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical reports.

claim: The white dots are not present at an early age and only become prominent in the teens and early adulthood, and slowly disappear with age.
source: The white dots are not present at an early age (Gränse et al., 2001) and only become prominent in the teens and early adulthood, and slowly disappear with age (Burstedt et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical reports.

claim: The macular sparing suggests that the white dots are more likely to be associated with rod photoreceptors.
source: The macular sparing suggests that these structures are more likely to be associated with rod photoreceptors.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that white dots are absent in the fovea, which is cone-rich.

claim: The white dots could represent retinyl ester-filled, enlarged retinosomes.
source: Based on the localization of these structures between the photoreceptor and RPE layer upon OCT imaging and the fact that other visual cycle defects (e.g., mutations in RDH5, RPE65) result in a similar punctate fundus appearance, we suggest that they could represent retinyl ester-filled, enlarged retinosomes, similar to the ones we found in the zebrafish retina.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the similarity of the phenotypes and the biochemical findings.

claim: Despite an accumulation of retinyl esters, Rlbp1−/− mice were not reported to have enlarged retinosomes or similar structures.
source: If this and their association with rod photoreceptors, as mentioned above, holds true, it is curious, that despite an accumulation of retinyl esters, Rlbp1−/− mice were not reported to have enlarged retinosomes or similar structures.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the literature.

claim: The larval retina nicely mimics the environment of foveal cones, even if rods are not completely absent.
source: First, considering cone density, the larval retina nicely mimics the environment of foveal cones, even if rods are not completely absent.
evidence: This is inferred from the known cone-dominant nature of the larval zebrafish retina.

claim: At 5 dpf, the accumulation of retinyl esters was not very pronounced yet and the number of lesions was much lower than in older retinas.
source: At this age, the accumulation of retinyl esters was not very pronounced yet and the number of lesions was much lower than in older retinas.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data (Figure 2B) and histological quantification (Figure 5H).

claim: Juvenile and adult retinas of zebrafish are cone rich but contain roughly 40 % of rods that are regularly interspersed throughout the retina.
source: On the other hand, juvenile and adult retinas of zebrafish are cone rich but contain roughly 40 % of rods that are regularly interspersed throughout the retina (Fadool, 2003) in contrast to the localized distribution in humans.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fadool, 2003.

claim: The older zebrafish retina resembles more the outer macular region.
source: The older zebrafish retina, therefore, resembles more the outer macular region.
evidence: This is inferred from the photoreceptor composition of the zebrafish retina.

claim: Complementary pathways for cones are thought to help them compete for available chromophores with the more abundant rod photoreceptors in the human retina.
source: Complementary pathways for cones are thought to help them compete for available chromophores with the more abundant rod photoreceptors in the human retina.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the field.

claim: The density of rods peaks just outside of the macular region.
source: The density of rods peaks just outside of the macular region.
evidence: This is stated as anatomical knowledge of the human retina.

claim: The high rod density outside the macular region is likely to exacerbate the need for alternative and larger chromophore sources.
source: This is likely to exacerbate the need for alternative and larger chromophore sources.
evidence: This is inferred from the competition for chromophores between rods and cones.

claim: The dramatic increase of enlarged retinosomes at the age of 1 month seems in line with the hypothesis that the white puncta are associated with the presence of rods.
source: The dramatic increase of enlarged retinosomes at the age of 1 month seems therefore in line with the hypothesis that the white puncta are associated with the presence of rods.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal correlation between rod development and retinsome accumulation.

claim: The different visual cycle pathways in RPE and MGC would be fine-tuned according to the type of cells they are in contact with.
source: It seems likely, that the different visual cycle pathways in RPE and MGC would be fine-tuned according to the type of cells they are in contact with.
evidence: This is a speculation about the regulation of visual cycle pathways.

claim: Single-cell transcriptomic analysis of the human retina and RPE revealed differences in peripheral and macular gene expression.
source: In line with this idea, single-cell transcriptomic analysis of the human retina and RPE (Voigt et al., 2019a; Voigt et al., 2019b) revealed differences in peripheral and macular gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Voigt et al., 2019a and 2019b.

claim: MGC-expressed RLBP1 has higher importance in the peripheral retina compared to the fovea.
source: Based on these datasets (Kiser and Palczewski, 2021) suggested higher importance for MGC-expressed RLBP1 in the peripheral retina compared to the fovea.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kiser and Palczewski, 2021.

claim: The MGC-mediated cycle may become more important in later stages with the increase of rod contribution.
source: The MGC-mediated cycle may become more important in later stages with the increase of rod contribution as it was previously suggested in Fleisch et al., 2008.
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to Fleisch et al., 2008.

claim: The absence of an ERG phenotype in rlbp1b−/− larvae could be explained by the MGC-mediated cycle becoming more important in later stages.
source: This could explain the absence of an ERG phenotype in rlbp1b−/− larvae and the only subtle changes in the capacity of double-KO (compared to rlbp1a−/−) to respond to strong bleaching lights and to recover thereafter.
evidence: This is a speculation to explain the observed phenotypes.

claim: The knockout of rlbp1b may have a more pronounced effect on retinal function at later stages when rods are more abundant.
source: It remains to be determined whether the knockout of rlbp1b will have a more pronounced effect on retinal function at later stages when rods are more abundant.
evidence: This is a speculation about future experiments.

claim: Cralbpb influenced the retinyl ester storage in adult rlbp1b−/− and double-KO.
source: But it is worthwhile to mention that Cralbpb influenced the retinyl ester storage in adult rlbp1b−/− and double-KO in the present study.
evidence: This is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 2C and E.

claim: Differences in density and distribution of photoreceptors and the expression pattern or activity of visual cycle proteins could in part explain the discrepancies between different animal models with mutations in CRALBP.
source: Differences in density and distribution of photoreceptors and the expression pattern or activity of visual cycle proteins could in part explain the discrepancies between different animal models with mutations in CRALBP.
evidence: This is a speculation about the reasons for differences between animal models.

claim: The differences in 11cisRE content between species might add to the discrepancies between animal models.
source: Also, the differences in 11cisRE content between species might add to this.
evidence: This is a speculation about the reasons for differences between animal models.

claim: The light environment to which the photoreceptors are exposed during life (nocturnal vs. diurnal species) may contribute to the phenotype.
source: In addition, the light environment to which the photoreceptors are exposed during life (nocturnal vs. diurnal species) may contribute to the phenotype.
evidence: This is a speculation about the reasons for differences between animal models.

claim: Species-specific differences may provide an explanation for the absence of subretinal lipid droplets in mouse eyes.
source: Together, these species-specific differences may provide an explanation for the absence of subretinal lipid droplets in mouse eyes.
evidence: This is a speculation about the reasons for differences between animal models.

claim: Knockout of RPE-expressed rlbp1a in zebrafish recapitulates the functional impairment and degenerative phenotype in RLBP1 disease.
source: In conclusion, knockout of RPE-expressed rlbp1a in zebrafish recapitulates the functional impairment and degenerative phenotype in RLBP1 disease.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results showing similar phenotypes in the zebrafish model and human patients.

claim: The zebrafish model shows an increase in retinyl esters and enlarged retinosomes, providing an explanation for the yellow-white fundus lesions commonly found in RLBP1 patients.
source: Importantly, our model shows an increase in retinyl esters and enlarged retinosomes, providing an explanation for the yellow-white fundus lesions commonly found in RLBP1 patients (see Figure 9 for a graphical overview of our working model).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between the biochemical and histological findings in the zebrafish model and the clinical observations in patients.

claim: The zebrafish model is an excellent model to further dissect the disease mechanism and to develop potential cures for RLBP1-associated disease.
source: It is therefore an excellent model not only to further dissect the disease mechanism, but also to develop potential cures for RLBP1-associated disease.
evidence: This is a claim about the utility of the model based on its recapitulation of human disease features.
